elements.element: Customer (IBM) may assign the Agreement to an affiliate without Vendor (MSL) consent.
elements.evidence: The added language states that “IBM may assign this Agreement without MSL's approval to an affiliate of IBM.”

elements.element: Customer (IBM) may assign the Agreement without Vendor (MSL) consent to a successor in a merger.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without MSL approval “to a successor in a merger.”

elements.element: Customer (IBM) may assign the Agreement without Vendor (MSL) consent to a successor in an acquisition.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without MSL approval “to a successor in an…acquisition.”

elements.element: Customer (IBM) may assign the Agreement without Vendor (MSL) consent to a successor in a sale of substantially all of IBM's assets.
elements.evidence: IBM may assign without MSL approval to a successor in a “sale of substantially all of its assets.”

elements.element: Vendor (MSL) may not assign the Agreement without Customer (IBM) consent.
elements.evidence: The original operative language requires IBM's prior written approval for MSL assignments, and the added language preserves IBM approval for assignments other than the absolute competitor prohibition.

elements.element: Customer's consent to a Vendor assignment may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The added language states that “IBM's approval of any other assignment by MSL shall not be unreasonably withheld.”

elements.element: Vendor (MSL) may never assign the Agreement to a Customer (IBM) competitor.
elements.evidence: The added language expressly states that “MSL may not assign this Agreement to any competitor of IBM.”

elements.element: Customer's change of control does not give Vendor a right to terminate the Agreement.
elements.evidence: The added language expressly provides that “no change of control of IBM shall give MSL any right to terminate this Agreement.”

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor without Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: IBM is expressly permitted to assign without MSL approval to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets.

elements.element: Customer must give Vendor written notice of an assignment to a successor.
elements.evidence: No operative provision requires IBM to provide MSL written notice of a successor assignment.

elements.element: Vendor may assign the Agreement to a successor without Customer consent.
elements.evidence: MSL remains subject to IBM's prior written approval. The requirement that a resulting company assume responsibility does not authorize assignment without consent.

elements.element: Vendor must give Customer written notice of an assignment to a successor.
elements.evidence: MSL must “immediately notify” IBM of specified transactions, but the clause does not require that notice to be written.

elements.element: Customer assignments other than assignments to successors require Vendor consent.
elements.evidence: The affiliate carve-out allows IBM to assign to an affiliate without MSL consent even where that affiliate is not a successor.

elements.element: Vendor consent to Customer assignments other than assignments to successors may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: The opening provision requires MSL approval for assignments generally but does not state that MSL's approval may not be unreasonably withheld.

elements.element: Vendor assignments other than assignments to successors require Customer consent.
elements.evidence: The clause states that MSL may not assign or transfer rights or duties without IBM's prior written approval; competitor assignments are additionally prohibited.

elements.element: Customer consent to Vendor assignments other than assignments to successors may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: IBM's approval may not be unreasonably withheld for assignments other than competitor assignments, but competitor assignments are categorically prohibited. Thus the standard does not apply to every non-successor assignment.

result.reason: The added language supplies every preferred substantive right and restriction and adds no unrelated commercial requirement. The fallback is not satisfied because successor-assignment rights are not mutual, written notice is omitted, IBM retains an affiliate carve-out, and competitor assignments are outside the generally applicable consent standard. Drafting quality is reduced because the new IBM no-consent rights facially conflict with the opening mutual-consent prohibition without an express “notwithstanding” or exception formulation, creating avoidable interpretive tension.
